subject: history
subtitle: How Britain was transformed by industrialisation from 1750, reshaping work, towns, and society.

data.targetWord: the process by which an economy changes from being mainly based on farming and hand production to being based on factories, machines and mass production

examples.en-GB: Industrialisation transformed Britain from a farming society into a factory nation during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

data.targetWord: a way of making goods, especially textiles, in people's homes or small workshops, where families worked together using hand tools or simple machines

examples.en-GB: Under the domestic system, a family might spin or weave cloth at home before delivering the finished product to a merchant.

data.targetWord: a way of making goods in large buildings where workers operated machines owned by an employer, following strict factory hours and rules

examples.en-GB: The factory system meant workers could no longer set their own pace; machines and overseers controlled the speed of production.

data.targetWord: the growth of towns and cities as more people move from rural areas to urban areas to find work

examples.en-GB: Urbanisation meant Manchester grew from around 20,000 people in 1750 to over 300,000 by 1851.

data.targetWord: a person who sets up and runs a business, often taking financial risks in the hope of making profit

examples.en-GB: Richard Arkwright was a successful entrepreneur who invested in factory production at Cromford Mill.

data.targetWord: money or wealth used to start, grow or invest in a business

examples.en-GB: Entrepreneurs needed capital to build factories and purchase expensive machinery.

data.targetWord: power produced by steam engines, which used heat, water and coal to create motion that could drive factory machinery and locomotives

examples.en-GB: James Watt's improvements to the steam engine made it efficient enough to power factories rather than just pumping water from mines.

data.targetWord: the use of machines to do work that had previously been done by hand or by animals

examples.en-GB: The mechanisation of spinning meant one worker could produce many times more thread than a hand-spinner.

data.targetWord: the major improvement in transport during the Industrial Revolution, including better roads, canals, steamships and railways

examples.en-GB: The transport revolution reduced the cost of moving coal and raw materials between industrial towns.

data.targetWord: natural resources used to make goods, such as cotton, coal, iron ore and wool

examples.en-GB: Cotton was one of the most important raw materials for Britain's textile factories during the Industrial Revolution.

data.targetWord: making large numbers of goods using machines and a divided labour force, so that costs fall and output rises

examples.en-GB: Mass production in textile factories meant cotton cloth became cheaper and more widely available to consumers.

data.targetWord: the employment of children in factories, mines or workshops, often for long hours in dangerous conditions

examples.en-GB: The 1833 Factory Act limited child labour in textile factories and required factory inspectors to check conditions.

data.targetWord: a machine invented by James Hargreaves in the 1760s that allowed one worker to spin several threads at once, increasing textile output

examples.en-GB: The spinning jenny increased the speed of thread production but was small enough to be used in homes or small workshops.

data.targetWord: a machine patented by Richard Arkwright in 1769 that used water power to spin stronger thread, requiring factory production near rivers

examples.en-GB: The water frame needed fast-flowing rivers, which is why Arkwright built his first mill at Cromford on the River Derwent.

data.targetWord: a machine developed by Samuel Crompton in 1779 that combined features of earlier spinning machines to produce fine, strong yarn

examples.en-GB: The spinning mule produced yarn strong enough for very fine cotton textiles, giving British cloth a competitive advantage.

data.targetWord: information about a source's origin: who made it, when, where, why and for whom, which affects how historians evaluate its usefulness

examples.en-GB: Considering the provenance of a factory report helps us decide whether the author had reason to present conditions more or less favourably.

data.targetWord: a view or explanation of the past that historians construct using evidence; different historians may interpret the same events differently

examples.en-GB: One interpretation of the Industrial Revolution focuses on progress and wealth, while another focuses on the suffering of factory workers.

data.targetWord: an artificial waterway built to transport heavy goods such as coal and raw materials more cheaply than by road

examples.en-GB: The Bridgewater Canal, opened in 1761, helped move coal more cheaply to Manchester, lowering fuel prices for factories.

data.targetWord: a law that banned children under nine from textile factories, limited working hours for older children and introduced factory inspectors

examples.en-GB: The Factory Act 1833 did not end child labour completely, but it was an important early step towards protecting children in the workplace.

data.targetWord: a law that banned women and girls, and boys under ten, from working underground in coal mines

examples.en-GB: The Mines Act 1842 was passed after parliamentary investigations revealed the dangerous conditions children faced underground.

data.targetWord: cloth or fabric; the textile industry was one of the first to be transformed by machines and factory production during the Industrial Revolution

examples.en-GB: Cotton textiles were central to early industrialisation because demand for cloth was high and new machines could speed up production.

data.targetWord: in factories, strict rules about timekeeping, behaviour and speed of work, enforced through fines and punishments

examples.en-GB: Factory discipline was much stricter than the domestic system because employers needed workers to keep pace with machinery.

data.targetWord: a group of territories controlled by one country; Britain's empire supplied raw materials and markets that contributed to industrialisation

examples.en-GB: Britain's empire provided cotton from overseas plantations, which fed the growing textile factories of Lancashire.

data.targetWord: a track along which steam-powered trains could move goods and passengers quickly, connecting industrial towns and transforming transport from the 1820s

examples.en-GB: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830, demonstrated that steam-powered railways could move goods and passengers efficiently.

data.targetWord: the health and wellbeing of an entire community, including clean water, sewers, and disease prevention, which became a concern as industrial towns grew

examples.en-GB: The 1848 Public Health Act was an early national response to the public health problems caused by overcrowded industrial towns.

data.targetWord: improvements in farming such as crop rotation and selective breeding that helped feed a growing population and contributed to industrialisation

examples.en-GB: Agricultural change helped feed Britain's growing industrial workforce and released some rural workers to seek wage work in factories.

data.targetWord: another name for the domestic system, where merchants supplied raw materials to home workers and collected finished goods

examples.en-GB: Under the putting-out system, a merchant supplied wool to cottage workers who spun it and returned the finished thread for payment.

data.sentence: The process by which an economy shifts from farming and hand production to factories and machines is called ____.
When workers made goods at home or in small workshops, this was known as the ____ system.
James Hargreaves is credited with inventing the spinning ____, which allowed one worker to spin multiple threads at once.
Richard Arkwright patented the water ____, which used river power to spin stronger thread inside factories.
James ____ improved the steam engine, making it efficient enough to power factory machinery and locomotives.
The Bridgewater ____, opened in 1761, helped move coal more cheaply from the mines to Manchester.
The 1833 Factory Act introduced factory ____ to check working conditions for children in textile factories.
Industrial towns faced serious problems including overcrowding, polluted water and outbreaks of diseases like ____.
Money or wealth used to invest in a business or factory is called ____.
The Liverpool and Manchester ____, opened in 1830, showed that steam power could transform transport of people and goods.
The 1842 Mines Act banned women, girls, and boys under ____ from working underground in coal mines.
The growth of towns and cities as people moved from rural areas to find factory work is called ____.
Abraham Darby used ____ rather than charcoal to smelt iron at Coalbrookdale, helping to make iron production cheaper.
A person who sets up and runs a business, taking financial risks in hope of making a profit, is called an ____.
Factories were first built near rivers because they needed ____ power before steam engines became widely available.
Britain's industrial growth was linked to empire because colonies supplied ____ such as cotton and provided markets for finished goods.
Samuel Crompton developed the spinning ____ in 1779, which produced fine, strong yarn combining features of earlier spinning machines.

data.title: Put these key events of the Industrial Revolution in chronological order.
items: James Watt patented improvements to the steam engine (1769)
Factory Act limited child labour in textile factories (1833)
Mines Act banned women and children from underground work (1842)

Entrepreneurs build mills and invest capital
More workers move to industrial towns
Production rises and goods become cheaper
Towns grow but overcrowding and pollution increase
Reformers campaign for factory and public health laws
